lesson.title: Dreams, demons and closure

lead.text: Descartes began his Meditations of 1641 by asking how much of what he believed he could really rely on. Most of it came through the senses, and the senses sometimes mislead: a stick looks bent in water, and a tower seen from far off looks round. These mistakes are easy to spot afterwards, so they do not seem serious.

Dreams are harder. While you dream you take what you see for real, and nothing in the dream announces that it is one. Descartes sat by his fire in a dressing gown, quite sure he was awake, and still could not name a sign that would separate waking from sleeping with certainty. If he could be asleep at that moment, nothing the senses seemed to show him was guaranteed.

The dream leaves something standing, though. Two and three make five whether you are awake or asleep, and a square has four sides either way. A dream can explain how the senses lead us astray, but arithmetic does not depend on the senses. To reach it, the doubt would have to go further.

So Descartes imagined something stronger than a dream. Suppose that a demon of great cunning and power has set out to deceive him, so that everything he seems to see and hear is an illusion the demon has planted. The same demon could make him go wrong every time he adds two and three.

This is the first example of what philosophers call a sceptical hypothesis: a story on which things seem exactly as they do now but are not as they seem. Nothing in your experience can refute such a story, because the story says your experience is what is being faked. A dream is a mild version. A modern version has you as a brain kept alive in a vat, fed signals by a computer.

Descartes found one thing the demon cannot touch. To be deceived at all, there must be someone who is deceived. Whatever else is false, he exists while he is being fooled, so “I exist” survives the strongest doubt he could devise. That gave him a place to start building, but it left ordinary knowledge of the world, such as knowing that you have hands, exposed.
Compare what a dream could make us doubt with what the demon could.

Modern sceptics do not ask you to believe in a demon. They put the demon to work inside an argument, and the argument starts from an ordinary thought. Say you claim to know that the shop on the corner is open. If you know that, you must also know that it has not burned down overnight, because a burned-down shop is not open. Hardly anyone objects to this step. When you know something and you know that it guarantees something else, you know the other thing too. Philosophers call this principle closure, since what you know stays closed under what you can see it guarantees.

Now apply it to yourself. Having hands rules out being a handless victim of the demon, so closure says that if you know you have hands, you know you are not being deceived. The sceptic then adds a second premise: you cannot know you are not being deceived, because a deception that works feels exactly like no deception.

Logicians shorten this by letting p stand for “I know I have hands” and q for “I know I am not deceived”. Closure supplies the first premise, if p then q, written p → q. The second premise says q is false, written ¬q. The conclusion is that p is false, written ¬p, which means you do not know you have hands. The next screen checks whether that conclusion really follows.
Test the shape as you would any argument: look for a case where both premises hold and the conclusion fails.

reveal.text: You tested the shape. The form p → q, ¬q, so ¬p is called modus tollens, and it has no counterexample row, so the argument is valid. A reply has to reject a premise.

steps.headline: Testing a form row by row

lead.text: Looking for a counterexample by imagination is quick, but a truth table makes the check mechanical. With two letters there are four rows, one for each way that p and q can be true or false. An argument form is valid when no row makes every premise true and the conclusion false, and a row that does is a counterexample.

Try the method on a tempting variant: if p then q, not p, so not q. The second premise is true only in the rows where p is false, which leaves two rows, one with q true and one with q false. The conditional p → q is true in both, since a conditional whose first part is false cannot fail. In the row where q is true, the conclusion not q is false. That row has true premises and a false conclusion, so the variant is invalid.

The sceptic's own form takes the same steps with different premises, and the practice question asks for the count. The result decides whether the sceptic can be answered by finding a fault in the logic.

lead.text: A valid argument leaves two choices: accept its conclusion or reject one of its premises. The sceptic's form is modus tollens, from “if p then q” and “not q” to “not p”, and a valid form cannot be answered by finding a fault in the logic. G. E. Moore, a Cambridge philosopher, took the second choice in 1939. In a paper called “Proof of an External World” he held up his hands and said, “Here is one hand.”

Moore kept the first premise and reversed the second. Instead of “I do not know I am not deceived” he began from “I know I have hands”. From p → q and p, the conclusion q follows by modus ponens, the mirror image of modus tollens: from “if p then q” and p, infer q. It is valid for the same reason as the sceptic's argument, since no row makes the premises true and the conclusion false.

So there are two valid arguments that share their first premise and end in opposite conclusions. Validity cannot settle the dispute, because both arguments have it. The question becomes which second premise deserves more trust, the sceptic's “I do not know I am not deceived” or Moore's “I know I have hands”. Moore said he was more certain of his hands than of any philosophical premise that could be set against them.

lead.text: Moore kept closure and denied the sceptic's second premise. There is another way out, which goes after the first premise instead. Fred Dretske and Robert Nozick, writing in the 1970s and 1980s, started from what it takes to know something. To know that you have hands, they said, your belief must be tied to the facts: if you did not have hands, you would not believe that you did. For ordinary people that tie holds.

Now take the claim that you are not a handless brain in a vat. If you were such a brain, you would still believe that you were not, because the vat feeds you the same experiences as before. Your belief is not tied to the fact in the same way, so Dretske and Nozick say that you cannot know it.

They accept the sceptic's second premise and they say that you know you have hands. Those two verdicts clash with the sceptic's first premise, and they accept that clash. In their view you can know one thing without knowing something it guarantees. The price is that this sounds odd: you know you have hands, yet you do not know you are not a handless brain in a vat.
Dretske and Nozick accept that you know you have hands. They deny that you can know you are not a handless brain in a vat.
Ask which general principle about knowledge those two verdicts contradict.

reveal.text: That principle is closure: if you know p, and know that p entails q, you know q. The sceptic's first premise is an instance of it, and Dretske and Nozick pay for their reply by giving it up.

blocks.text: Last lesson ended with a sceptic, someone who says we know far less than we think. This lesson gives the sceptic a proper hearing, and it starts somewhere harmless. Almost everyone has had a dream so vivid that waking up came as a surprise.

That ordinary experience is the seed of one of philosophy's oldest worries. If a dream can feel exactly like waking life, no feeling can prove to you that you are awake. Descartes pushed the worry much further in 1641, and later philosophers squeezed it into an argument short enough to write on a card.
We follow the worry from the dream to that argument. Then we test whether the argument is valid, and look at the ways philosophers have tried to get out of it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll test the sceptic's argument for validity and say which premise Moore, Dretske and Nozick each reject.

recap.keyIdea: The sceptic's argument is valid, so it can only be answered by rejecting a premise. Moore trusts his hands over the sceptic's second premise. Dretske and Nozick give up closure.

blocks.text: You began with a dream and pushed the doubt out to a demon. The doubt then became a short argument, which you tested row by row before comparing the replies of Moore, Dretske and Nozick.

recap.nextHook: The sceptic treats knowing as all or nothing, but most doubt comes in degrees. The next lesson asks how a piece of evidence should change how confident you are.
